entry.title: The Best New Books for Kids Published in 2026
entry.summary: The year’s best picture books, chapter books, graphic novels, and nonfiction.
entry.content:
This was another banner year for children’s books, with creators exploring new formats, expansive styles of illustration, and complex themes in inventive ways. Many stories take place in imagined worlds, where kids escape from reality or use their ingenuity to solve problems in fantastical lands. Others connect us with the magic and awe found in nature. Here are some excellent new titles published in 2026 that would be great gifts for the kids in your life. They come recommended by artists, writers, parents, bookstore owners, and children’s-book creators, all of whom have spent countless hours reading to kids.

Anna Watanabe, a co-founder of Do Re Mi Books, a new publisher based out of the U.K., recommends this playful board book for toddlers that inspires play. “As you read along, it invites little ones to pretend to be a feline friend. It’s perfect for any cat lover, with gorgeous illustrations by Japanese artist Yoshiko Hada.”

“This charming story follows a red truck befriended by a small child, carrying it with them at all times,” says Caroline Rodrigues, owner of the beloved children’s shop Merci Milo, which has just opened a new location in Brooklyn. It’s Jon Klassen’s follow-up to his Your Places box set, recommended last year.

Also illustrated by Klassen and written by his longtime collaborator, Mac Barnett, “This box set is a beautiful object, but it’s also a fine example of the possibilities of the board book as an art form,” says Taylor Sterling, author of Moonbow, a newsletter about children’s books. “Each book pays poetic attention to a season: what kids might notice, how it feels and changes, but the most thrilling thing is what kids will notice when reading the books all together — where the same words with new images create a different visual and visceral experience.”

Sam Voulters, author of How to Be a Cat, recommends this playful book with its bold paper collage illustrations for the youngest readers. “With an international menu, including PB&J, masala toast from India, and even British beans on toast, it’s a great first book about food.”

“This book is a celebration of the power of using what we have, working with our hands, and making something useful and meaningful in the process,” says Erin Boyle, the writer and creative behind Make/Do and co-author of Making Things. “Phoebe Wahl absolutely nails the illustrations, highlighting the subtle and brilliant ways the book challenges gendered expectations and norms — a braiding boy, a sewing dad — to spread the message that craft and handwork is for everyone!”

“This book would make a great bedtime story for restless children or for those who challenge the idea of sleep,” says illustrator Ping Zhu, who has two recently published books — Animals of the Chinese Zodiac, by Teresa Robeson, and The Story of Art Without Men: an Illustrated Guide, by Katy Hessel. “Full of humor and playfulness, it’s a departure from sleep being something to fear into a thing of a wonder.”

In another sleep-themed book, recommended by Mallory Neidich, owner of Spiral Books, “Saehan Parc imagines sleep as a sprightly, curious creature who flits around the world with a sleep-inducing wand. Playful, funny, and imaginative, it’s an ideal book to read before bed, and the hand-stencilled illustrations are stunning.”

“This charming story takes you through a strange town that comes alive at night,” says Zhu. The town is filled with all the imaginative and slightly ridiculous things kids might dream are happening at night, where the air smells like cinnamon and blueberries, and there are octopi and giant cats running about. “The intricately cut paper and painted collage makes this book endlessly entertaining to look at,” adds Zhu.

In Sid Sharp’s first picture book, following two fantastic graphic novels, Bog Myrtle and The Wolf Suit, she turns the bedtime story upside down with a creepy house full of nocturnal creatures who rise as the sun goes down and get up to all kinds of antics. “When there is so much ‘safe’ publishing for young kids, it’s great to enjoy something genuinely transgressive that so delights (my) children,” says Voulters.

Jess Hannigan’s latest (we recommended her previous book, The Bear Out There, in last year’s guide) has a cow wondering about the mysterious happenings of nighttime, a big theme of many of this year’s great books. “It has a lurid palette, bold cut-out illustrations, a naïve cow, and some untrustworthy nocturnal characters,” says Watanabe. “It’s also brimming with Hannigan’s hilarious voice.”

Seven curious ants set off to discover the world beyond their anthill in this exuberantly colorful story. “Yoon created the illustrations using pre-separation, an old-school printmaking technique, and the result is layered and textured and teeming with life. It’s a gorgeous story about adventure, curiosity, and finding the perfect home,” says Neidich.

This title features Worm, who is tired of being a librarian and ready to explore some other career options. But, being a worm, it’s hard to convince future employers that he’s the guy for the job. “This book is hilarious and so inventive,” says Sri Juneja, creator of Readable Moments. “It’s a heartwarming story that reminds kids that we all have our special skills; all you have to do is believe in yourself.”

“I love a children’s book that can help grown-ups and kids alike grapple with great big concepts — the climate crisis, immigration, and belonging — without either oversimplifying or getting overly didactic,” says Boyle, of this story that also follows the migration route of monarch butterflies. “I wish every classroom in America had a copy of this gorgeous book.”

In this gorgeous picture book, a young boy, mired in fever and home from school, follows a cricket through a crack in the wall on an unexpected adventure. “I love this inventive, imaginative story, from the way the number is incorporated into the narrative, to the subtle themes of care and empathy woven throughout,” says designer and illustrator Erin Jang. “And how incredible that Cordell created the illustrations solely using scented multicolored ballpoint pens from his kids’ art bin!” Kids who love the detailed, fine-line illustrations by Chris Van Allsburg or Aaron Becker are also likely to love this.

“This transformational picture book is a philosophical exploration of entrances both literal and metaphorical: doors, books, portals, thresholds — and celebrates the ingenious ways children use their imaginations to learn about the world and themselves,” says Sterling. ““Doors lead to parties, secret hiding spots, fantasy lands, and are entryways for a parade of cats,” adds author and artist Julia Rothman. “The full page illustrations are designed so graphically, even with their subtle handmade textures, utilizing bold shapes and white space on the page to let you know where she wants you to look next. This book is playful and poetic in all the best ways.”

This debut children’s book by Anna Haifisch, a German illustrator and cartoonist, subverts Aesop’s fable of the cricket and the ant. “It’s beautifully rendered in Pantone inks that fight with each other,” says Voulters. It’s a poignant tale exploring the power of music and art, told with lightness and humor that is just perfect for deep winter.

“If there were no words at all, I’d recommend this beautiful book just for getting lost in the illustrations,” says Boyle. “It’s a magical blend of science and wonder and creation myth — a quiet meditation on the enormity of the universe and our tiny place in it.” The book’s publisher, Claudia Bedrick, at Enchanted Lion Books, adds that this book “comes as the most generous invitation to feel the wonder and miracle of life.”

This tale, based on a true story, follows a daughter’s first-person recollection of her mother’s weather recording in Iceland and how she helps the community. “The illustrations about her mother’s journey are broken into panels on some spreads and reads like a painted comic, each more quietly captivating than the next,” says Rothman. “I like that it is ultimately about generations of women following a tradition of doing a job tied to the natural world.”

“This book is delightful and funny and asks big existential questions with humor kids will appreciate,” says Juneja, of this tale of friendship, loss, and the circle of life between a dinosaur and a worm. “It shows us the role we all play, whether we are big, small, or extinct. This is great for kids who love nature, dinosaurs, worms, and are just starting to ask big questions about the world around them.”

In this title from the Korean writer and illustrator Bonsoir Lune, watermelon isn’t just a fruit, it’s a destination, an escape from a hot day, and a swimming pool. An entire town, from the youngest to the eldest, gathers at a giant watermelon to cool off from the heat of summer, diving through its juicy flesh, making sweet slides, and wading through its seeds. The fantastical, yet gentle images of the town frolicking in the watermelon evoke a quiet playfulness and big imagination.

At the center of Dorléans’s story is a young boy who struggles with being afraid of everything: wind, rain, cats, loud sounds, and even dragonflies. He discovers a big, plush, red knit blanket, and this physical shield becomes a way — however symbolic — of facing the world. The illustrations, a combination of graphite and watercolor, show the intricacies of the tightly woven blanket being lugged around town. This book is perfect for lovers of Extra Yarn by Mac Barnett, another fantastic book where yarn takes on outsize value.

A singing crew of moles comes to the rescue when the squirrel family’s treehouse begins to tilt. “This delightful book is translated from Japanese and painted in acrylics. I am always on the lookout for beautifully done, construction-themed books, and this one fits the bill,” says Neidich.

“How fun to have a main character you never actually see! You see a floating hat or the blush on their cheeks in the mirror, but you never see the whole ghost character until the end,” says Rothman. “The ghost is worried they won’t have things to talk about with other guests, a classic worry anyone can relate to, and they ask the reader if they can practice small talk with them.” In addition to the clever premise, Rothman notes the impact of the illustrations: “The soft-toned glowing scenes are magical to begin with, and with this extra layer of imagining the ghost, it’s a real delight.”

“This deliciously old-fashioned book provides kids hours of fun, creativity, projects, and delight,” says Bedrick. It’s the second in a new two-book series by Green, taking place over the seasons, with best friends Henri and Miko exploring the seasons in their wooded village. Channeling Beatrix Potter and Chirri and Chirra, this book celebrates friendship and nature.

“The soft, hazy illustrations give so much coziness to this lovely little story about two children who live nearby but have never met, until one day, they do,” says Juneja. “There’s a poignancy to the notion of lives that run parallel and then, magically, seem to intersect. Kids will love identifying all the times Tom and Momo are in the same place, at the same time but never meet.” Bedrick, who also recommends this title, says, “This wintry tale is calm and utterly charming. Readers will lose themselves again and again for long, happy stretches.”

This story’s protagonist is Home, an actual house, who misses its occupant Poppy. She’s a young girl who has gone to her G-pa and Mimi’s house and is out collecting pinecones and baking bread, leaving Home feeling bad. “Color is used so masterfully to show the contrast between Poppy’s adventure (in warm colors like pink, coral) and Home’s longing (in blues),” says Rothman. “Poppy wakes up homesick and when she arrives back Home, the pages explode in warm colors again. I really love the flip-flop of a house missing its inhabitant, and I’m so impressed with how a palette could be used to help portray emotion.”

“This picture book conjures an entire world where mushroom elves, dragon slayers, and spirits dwell. The ink-wash illustrations are breathtaking, and the storytelling is vivid and detailed (think Alice in Wonderland meets Spirited Away),” says Neidich. “It’s the first in a series of seven books translated from Chinese and published by Elsewhere Editions, one of my absolute favorite publishers.”

“Warren beautifully captures the sense of feeling adrift that some kids may experience at the start of a life change — and what’s a bigger life change than starting middle school?” says Afoma Umesi, creator of Reading Middle Grade. “At its heart, this is a sweet friendship story with a heartfelt nod to the love of filmmaking that will resonate with fans of Raina Telgemeier. It’s for those navigating identity and belonging, but also for those who love to daydream and create.”

“A hilarious new graphic-novel series about a ‘fishboy’ who tries to pass as a regular kid at an elementary school in a mysterious town where his relative, ‘the Beast of Barnacle Bay,’ lurks,” says Sterling. “Sashimi’s mission to find someone who looks like him gets more and more wild as he and his new friends hunt for the mythical creature and discover something he never expected. This book is perfect for kids who like Dog Man, Captain Underpants, and Diary of a Wimpy Kid. It’s fast-paced and packed with humor and heart.”

This graphic novel about a young girl who unexpectedly finds herself joining a coding club in middle school “is semi-autobiographical, based on the life of author Samara Mehta, founder of the coding game CoderBunnyz,” says book critic and editor Lauren LeBlanc. “It’s a good story about friendship and belonging. A resourceful Sama must devise creative strategies to gain the respect of her peers and earn her place on the team. The book celebrates the rewards of perseverance.”

Fans of Blabey’s Bad Guys series will jump right into this silly story of a boy who learns that he’s been chosen to save the world from a sinister plot instigated by pets. “This book is the perfect mix of lightly spooky and wildly funny,” says Umesi. “In the author-illustrator’s trademark style, the black-and-white illustrations add to the emotion of the story, from the humans’ anxious expressions to the mischief on the pets’ faces.”

Aficionados of the original Baby-Sitters Club series by Ann M. Martin will recall there are 15 “super special” books in the series, featuring narration from every member of the BSC. In this first graphic-novel adaptation, Telgemeier and Galligan, who wrote and illustrated other graphic novels in the series, team up on this adventure that takes Kristy, Claudia, Mary Anne, Stacey, Dawn, Mallory, and Jessi on a summer vacation filled with child-rearing responsibilities, crushes, and much more.

Umesi also recommends this title for “readers familiar with Layton’s The Academy series.” This newest book dives into the world of volleyball and the dynamics of high school. “Think of it as the Karate Kid but with volleyball, a teen girl, and her estranged father. Layton’s pacing never lets up, making this a one-sitting read.”

“Chock-full of interesting details, this book is a great book for readers of her previous novel, Magnolia Wu Unfolds It All, who are ready for a more mature book. It deals with growing pains and friendship conflict through the eyes of a reflective and sensitive narrator,” says LeBlanc.

“Amy is the author of my first picture book, The Strange Birds of Flannery O’Connor, and writes in a way that boldly leads readers into a new world,” says Zhu. Nash, a 12-year-old, self-proclaimed cowboy longs for a real horse, but must navigate the complexity of family, friendships, and feelings as she navigates adolescence. “It’s completely engaging, tenderly told, and masterfully paced,” says Bedrick. “It’s a great gift for any young reader who marches to their own beat and is looking for adventure,” adds Zhu.

In this middle-grade novel, Giles writes of a seventh-grader grappling with the news that a beloved teacher has been inappropriate with some students. “I love the way the story shows young readers what grooming can look like and demonstrates why speaking up can be challenging but how vital it is to do so,” says Umesi. “Impressively, this summer-set story never feels weighed down by its subject matter and ends on an inspiring, hopeful note.”

Sara Pennypacker’s latest novel is for young history buffs and kids who enjoy stories about underdogs finding their own voice. “Set in 1940s France, this story is full of lesser-known facts about Nazi Germany’s atrocities, such as their mission to breed Aryan soldiers in rural France,” recommends Umesi.

This book seems to defy both logic and order, with chapters sequenced out of order and a story the reader must piece together. My 10-year-old daughter loved the tale as a read-aloud, following the story of an unlikely young goatkeeper, Bernadette, who must rescue 24 coats from a very volatile king with the help of a forgetful wizard. It’s full of adventure and silliness, and my daughter loved seeing how the rescue mission unfolded for this haphazard crew.

“Parents know that reading stage when their elementary-grade kid latches onto a series and has to read every single book from it from the library before moving on,” says Jang. “My kid is currently into James Ponti’s books. The latest (seventh) book in the City Spies series was a highly anticipated drop and has proved to be an exciting, entertaining read that my child can’t put down.”

The third book in the Impossible Creatures series, “Rundell’s characters are plucky and often hilarious as they face incredible challenges in the Archipelago, a land just beyond our own where mythical creatures roam,” says LeBlanc. “Questions of climate crisis and cruelty are ever-present in her books, but Rundell, who is quite outspoken regarding biodiversity and cautious of AI, doesn’t reduce her work to morality plays. The audiobooks, read by Samuel West, are also exceptional.”

The Swift kids, whose names are as quirky as the mischief they find themselves navigating, are back with a third installment. This time, Shenanigan and cousin Atrocious team up with the children of family friends (Basil, Moss, and Delphinium) and find themselves trapped in a greenhouse during a snowstorm with a murder mystery to solve. This series is great for lovers of wordplay, sleuthing, and absurd adventures.

For kids who like to spin yarns, dig into mysteries, and explore symbolism, this encyclopedia of superstitions digs into how each came to be. “It doesn’t just detail superstitions we’re familiar with, but we also learn of other superstitions from around the world,” says Juneja. “And the illustrations are vibrant and sassy and kids will learn cool things about superstitions and why we believe them.”

“My 15-year-old bird lover couldn’t wait to read through Julia Rothman’s latest book in The Anatomy Series,” says Jang. (All of the books in the series make for great gifts.) “The book is filled with beautiful hand-painted illustrations and a wide range of fascinating facts about birds. It’s presented in an easy, approachable way that engages both kids who are curious and new to birds and aspiring ornithologists.”

“I couldn’t have been more pleased when my 10-year-old discovered Calvin and Hobbes on our bookshelf and fell in love with Bill Watterson’s comics,” says Jang. “This one is the last set in this compact compendium. The smaller format is perfect for him to throw in his backpack and read on the bus to school.”

entry.title: The Strollers, Car Seats, and Carriers Strategist Parents Use for Travel
entry.summary: Traveling with kids is hard, but having the right gear makes it easier.
entry.content:
The most tantalizing advice I received as a new parent was to get an ambitious trip in early while the baby was still more asleep than awake and easier to carry around. This was how a short cross-country visit to introduce my 9-week-old daughter to my 86-year-old grandmother morphed into a weeklong road trip down and up the California coast. It was manageable, if not particularly enjoyable, and I wouldn’t advise anyone to do the same. However, I learned a lot about traveling with a baby in a short time, which I will gladly share — alongside the collective wisdom of my Strategist parent colleagues. Whether you’re planning a quick familial visit in the car or a multi-week international vacation with long-haul flights on either end, these are the car seats, boosters, strollers, and carriers we use to take our kids wherever they need to go.

The Cosco Scenera is a classic lightweight travel car seat for littler kids that six separate Strategist writers and editors have entrusted with their kids over the years. “It is good enough for the price and how lightweight it is,” says senior editor Jen Trolio. “Like to the point where it was absolutely reasonable to ship to a destination and leave it there, rather than try to rent or borrow one of unknown condition.” Senior editor Winnie Yang bought one while already at her trip destination, after Avis provided a car seat that wasn’t up to snuff. It may look simple, but it’s comfortable enough for longer road trips, according to Yang. Note that the Scenera does not have a no-rethread harness, which means you must take the time to adjust it correctly before leaving home. All the parents I spoke to reported their kids outgrew it by height faster than other car seats, but that’s a forgivable flaw at this price.

Once your child is big enough to safely use the Pico, it offers a huge portability upgrade. “It’s close to $500, but it’s absolutely worth it because it folds up,” says Strategist deals writer Martha Tuber of her Pico. “You can just put it over your shoulder and it’s just so easy to carry,” compared to a regular car seat. It only weighs eight pounds, which means you can take it almost anywhere, including on a golf cart in the Dominican Republic, as senior writer (and Strategist baby-gear correspondent) Liza Corsillo once did with her son: “He was able to ride on the back, facing out, with me sitting next to him, holding hands, and I wasn’t worried about him slipping or sliding off of the seat.” Yang used hers on planes and in cars and notes that it’s not the most comfortable because it’s rather upright. But when it comes to portability, “there’s really no substitute.” When her family uses it on a plane, her husband clips the Pico to the hiking backpack he uses as a carry-on with a carabiner to get through the airport at either end of the trip.

Once your kid has outgrown the need for a full car seat, Strategist senior editor Michael Berk recommends keeping this inflatable backless booster around for taxis and such: “It’s good for family holidays where you might end up in a childless cousin’s car.” Yang also recommends it, as long as your kid isn’t too squirmy. And Trolio keeps it around for shorter trips.

Upon learning of my wife’s pregnancy, Corsillo recommended we get the Joolz Aer2 for transporting our baby around the city. It’s been perfect on the streets of Brooklyn — and even more impressive on the road and in the air. The car seat adapters easily slotted into our Cybex Cloud T car seat, and I loved being able to fold the frame down to an overhead-bin-friendly size at the gate with one hand while carrying a tote bag full of baby stuff in the other. Even though strollers can be gate-checked for free, you never know what’s happening in the cargo hold, so it’s nice to carry it on for peace of mind. We left the fold-flat bassinet attachment at home during our trip but missed it dearly. Our baby prefers it to the car seat, and it provides an easy and safe way for sleep-deprived parents to carry a napping, floppy-necked infant around a room.

Deals writer Martha Tuber has been testing and loving this stroller with her 8-month-old, and it’s also been Corsillo’s primary stroller for her 4-year-old. “It has better or equal handling to the Joolz Aer2 and a slightly bigger basket underneath,” says Corsillo. Both moms appreciate how quickly it folds with one hand. Corsillo adds that the seat itself does a better job of cradling the child and the canopy extends a bit lower for additional shade — helpful for promoting napping. Parents of newborns and infants would still benefit from the Joolz’s bassinet attachment (Bugaboo doesn’t offer one for this stroller), but once the child has outgrown the bassinet, Corsillo prefers the Butterfly’s overall usability.

If you don’t mind a finicky four-step folding process, the Yoyo is a venerable design beloved by Europeans for its compact size and durability. “The Yoyo has been the best for us,” says Yang. “I prefer it also for using as our main stroller, especially once the kid is walking a lot, since it’s just easier to carry around folded — especially up and down subway stairs — than many other options. We used ours in Venice, going all around the cobblestones and over many bridges and onto vaporetti and water taxis, and I can’t imagine trying to do that with any other stroller.” Corsillo adds that there are better handling options that are easier to fold (such as the two above), but for the price, the Yoyo is a solid choice.

Ride-along luggage only works on perfectly smooth flooring, such as you’d find at an airport, so it’s not for everyday use. “This is my No. 1 travel hack; it makes the airport fun for my son,” says Corsillo. “He does not complain about waiting in line, and everybody compliments it.” She appreciates that it’s designed with an incline that keeps it stable so she doesn’t have to hold it at all times. “It doesn’t fit a ton of stuff,” she cautions, “but it was big enough for my clothes and his clothes for a short trip when he was a lot younger.”

“If you’re a carry-on-only family, use your gate-checked stroller bag for luggage overflow,” says Strategist senior editor Martin Mulkeen. Even if you don’t need an extra-large stroller cover, the bigger bag leaves more space for stowing your stuff. “We usually put about five pairs of shoes in with the stroller that can’t fit in regular luggage. Or it ends up filled with the stuff we bought on the trip,” he adds. Yang also did this (and used the hiking carrier backpack bag similarly), stuffing the extra space with a week’s worth of diapers, a baby carrier, winter coats — anything compressible. Just be aware that policies vary internationally. Mulkeen learned the hard way that inter-Europe flights send strollers to the baggage-claim area (though not on the carousel), “which is why all the Euro families have Yoyos, because they fit in the overhead compartment.”

The Pipa travel system is well liked by multiple Strategist staffers for newborns and infants. “I loved traveling with this car seat,” says deputy editor Simone Kitchens. “It’s super-easy to pop into any car and weighs nothing.” She particularly appreciates how the car seat locks into the stroller seat to create a “dome of darkness” that helps with napping, especially in a bright, noisy airport. Yang also liked this feature when she used it with her youngest.

Cybex’s Cloud car seats can expand into a nearly lie-flat, reclined position by unfurling the hard exterior, like a pill bug. (This is only possible outside of the car.) My typically even-keeled infant daughter detests car seats and usually starts screaming as soon as she’s buckled in. But as soon as we can take the seat off its base and recline it, the screaming stops and we can peacefully, comfortably mount it to the matching Balios stroller legs. The stroller itself is rather large, but the bigger wheels and softer suspension handle gravel and cobblestones much better than our Joolz Aer2. We also appreciate that the capacious cargo basket easily holds a week’s worth of groceries.

Unlike other travel systems, where the stroller and car seat are separate devices that come together as needed, the Doona’s stroller parts are designed to fold into the car seat like a transformer. It’s an impressively elegant solution that works really well for babies who need a rear-facing car seat and a parent-facing stroller, but it can’t grow with the child beyond this stage. Strategist lead editor Lauren Levy was a big fan of the original, which she says is especially useful for city parents who might not have cars and are going in and out of cabs and Ubers all the time. She’s been enjoying the new model’s higher-end materials and ability to recline.

This is one of the simplest carriers we’ve tested, and it’s a favorite of both Tuber and Corsillo. “It’s very soft and kind of molds to your body,” says Corsillo, “so it made it feel like he was really close and secure without feeling like it was squishing him too tightly.” In this way, it gives you a lot of the benefits of a wrap-style carrier without the hassle of actually having to tie a wrap.

With this carrier, I can wear my 15-pound infant strapped to my chest for hours without back pain, and once we’re back home, it’s easy to transfer her from my chest to the crib without needing a second set of hands. It’s adjustable enough to fit me comfortably at six-feet-two and my wife at five-feet-five, and we’ve been using it comfortably with our baby from eight pounds onward. The mesh shoulder straps and waist belt form a vest that securely hugs the torso. Then the baby harness attaches at four separate points using quick-release buckles that can be operated with one hand. This means I can hold her with one hand while unbuckling with the other. It’s a bit fussy to learn at first, but once I got the hang of it, it’s as fast as any other carrier. I also appreciate the ample use of mesh, which helped stave off heat exhaustion while walking around California in the recent autumnal heat wave. The somewhat finicky packable sunshade is also helpful here, since it’s apparently impossible to keep a hat on my baby’s head.

What do Rihanna, opera singer Lise Davidsen, and deals writer Martha Tuber all have in common? This carrier, of course. “I wish I could tell you that it’s all just hype and not worth it,” writes Tuber, “but, you guys, unfortunately the Zeitgeist carrier really is that great.” I’ve also been testing one out in Brooklyn and love how easy it is to put on and take off for short jaunts to the store or around the block. This is also why it’s my mother-in-law’s preferred carrier, even if it hurts her back after a while.

Yang’s husband’s carrier of choice is actually a hiking carrier. It takes everything Osprey knows about carrying many pounds of backpacking gear and translates it into a super-ergonomic kid carrier. “We only leave it at home if we know we’re not walking around, which is very rare,” says Yang. It weighs more than a cloth carrier, but it actually feels lighter because it’s engineered to take weight off of the back and shoulders and direct it onto the hips and legs. And since the baby isn’t actually pressed against your body, it’s more breathable, too. Note that your child must be able to support their own head before you can safely use this carrier.

Once your toddler can support their own head, you can safely switch to a simpler hip carrier. These typically have just one strap and buckle to deal with, so they’re much easier to put on and take off. Among those that Corsillo has tried, the Upsie is her favorite so far because it strikes the right balance between kid and parental comfort: “It cups the butt of a kid well but doesn’t have a big hard buckle,” which can dig uncomfortably into your hip. For a softer, albeit less supportive hip carrier, she recommends the Mabe Monarch.

Even if you have a carrier you like, Corsillo recommends keeping this packable carrier around as a just-in-case option. It packs into its own pocket so you can wear it like a fanny pack, but it’s also compact and light enough to throw into any bag on short notice so you’re not stuck without one.

entry.title: Everything You Need for a Power Outage, According to Experts
entry.summary: We talked to city officials and preppers to find everything you need to build a blackout kit.
entry.content:
When the power goes out, what you’ll need is a blackout kit (also called an emergency supply kit) containing all the things that’ll get you through an outage at home safely. Herman Schaffer, deputy commissioner for community engagement at the NYC Emergency Management Office, says that even though “a kit should be personalized to the needs of the specific individual,” there are essential items — your flashlights, headlamps, chargers, and first-aid kits — that every single person should have on hand. Because a power outage can be caused by any number of things — like a major winter snowstorm, for example — we talked to a range of experts, from city officials to apocalypse preppers, about what they would recommend stocking in a blackout kit to stay safe (and sane). For those who would prefer to handle the preparedness in one fell swoop, there are pre-stocked kits for that, too. For even more emergency-preparedness tips, check out our roundup here.

Updated on November 17, 2026
﻿We’ve updated this story by checking availability of the products listed, updating prices, and adding some new options.

Buying a premade emergency-preparedness kit is an option that can help you prepare for blackouts, as well as other emergency situations like extreme weather events and evacuations. According to former Strategist editor Maxine Builder, “These kits will help you and your family prepare for just about any disaster you might encounter, without expending too much extra effort on your end.” When Builder tested out several of these kits, she was impressed with this option from Ready America, which she calls “an excellent starter kit, especially given the price.” The lightweight backpack includes a first aid kit, water, light sticks, as well as other survival supplies. Builder did have this tip: “To make it your own, start by throwing out the bag and moving all the gear into a larger — and, ideally, more technical — backpack,” so you can add additional items that will suit the specific needs of your family.

If you’d rather stock your kit from scratch, our experts have plenty of advice. But before you start stocking your kit with supplies, Schaffer stresses that it is essential to keep your items in one centralized location so you can find everything you need — from a flashlight to backup medications — in the event of an emergency. This bin is weathertight to keep contents clean and dry. Plus, it is made of clear plastic, so you can easily see what’s inside.

Michael Clendenin, a retired spokesperson for Con Edison, recommends “stocking up on basic food supplies and water” for yourself and your pets, in the unlikely event that the outage lasts more than a few hours. The general rule of thumb, he says, is one gallon per person per day.

Jason Charles, president of the New York City Preppers Network, also likes this first aid kit from Thrive to treat minor injuries. However, he also recommends supplementing a standard first aid kit with your own medicine and personal products to suit your specific medical needs. On an additional health note, both Schaffer and Clendenin stressed that if you are a person who relies on assistance equipment that requires backup power, you should make sure you are registered with your utility company so that local authorities are aware of your needs.

Charles says a fire extinguisher “is a must-have, especially if you live in an apartment building that doesn’t have sprinklers.”

“We advise people to make sure you’ve got a portable battery for your phone,” says Clendenin, so that you can make emergency calls and have access to an additional flashlight and personal entertainment. Dale Goodwin, host of the Survivalist Prepper podcast, recommends portable chargers from Anker. The Nano is one of our favorite portable chargers for its built-in cable, making it convenient to carry without an extra cord.

Aaron Frankel, host of In the Rabbit Hole: Urban Survival Podcast, recommends stocking up on both AA and AAA batteries to power your flashlights, radios, and any other essentials that you’ll no longer be able to charge with a wall plug.

If you live with other people and want to be prepared for a longer outage, prepper Sharon Ross (who goes by Afrovivalist) recommends power stations from Goal Zero, which hoards enough power to quickly charge laptops as well as phones. It comes equipped with USB ports and regular outlets, and “you can charge it from a plug socket when your power is working fine,” says Ross.

The survivalists we spoke to cautioned that even batteries will eventually lose their power. Instead, for peace of mind, they recommended solar-panel chargers, which simply sit in a sunny place when you’re not using them and then provide hours of charging power should you need them in a crisis. They’ll work to recharge everything from cell phones, to external battery packs, to lanterns. Both Goodwin and Ross praised the solar chargers from Goal Zero in particular. “It’s fantastic,” Goodwin says, “because it comes with a solar panel, a battery bank, and a flashlight all in one.”

This solar generator from Jackery is another good option to have on hand. It’s compact and lightweight, has six output ports, and takes just two hours to charge it up to 80 percent capacity. (Actor Jay Duplass swears by it.)

This far more affordable solar-panel option — that charges your phone and works as a flashlight — came highly recommended to us by Charles.

Everyone we spoke to said that a light is, understandably, one of the most important items to stock in your kit. Charles says that when it comes to flashlights, a Maglite is “one of the most dependable lights on the market. They are sturdy, tough, and take batteries.”

While a flashlight is great for aiming your light, especially in nooks and crannies, almost all of our experts talked about the importance of keeping a headlamp nearby also. That’s because it frees up your hands in the dark, which makes essential tasks (or just reading in bed) easier to complete and prevents injuries because your hands are now free to catch you should trip or fall in the dark. (Schaffer adds that your headlamp should always be kept next to your bed so it’s easily accessible should the power go out when the sun’s also down.) Strategist senior writer Michael Zhao recommends this quick-charging headlamp from BioLite: “This extremely comfortable headlamp gains an hour of run time with just eight minutes of charging.”

Both Goodwin and Frankel keep glow sticks in their kits, which are a fun and effective way to light up your home, especially for kids (and the young at heart).

Coonradt and Hardy recommend this solar lighting system because it “is a great way to minimize the inconvenience” of a power outage “without spending a bunch of money on a generator.” Solar-generated light systems work much like solar chargers — according to Charles, “you let the panels charge in natural light during the day, then they produce good light at night.”

This affordable system includes a six-watt solar panel, three individual string lights, and three overhead lights (all with individual switches), a motion sensor, two USB device charging ports, a digital display for feedback on power availability, and a built-in FM radio and speaker. Plus, the battery holds a 20-hour charge.

Frankel also likes this rechargeable lantern that comes with a USB power hub.

A manual can opener is an often overlooked item, according to the experts we spoke to. “To many people’s surprise, when they go to enjoy their canned fruit cocktail when the power is out, they realize their electric can opener is useless. Having a manual can opener can literally save the day until power is restored,” explains Coonradt and Hardy. This one by OXO has an easy-to-turn knob and nonslip handles.

Schaffer recommends also keeping a safety whistle in your kit. “It helps you to alert people if you’re in trouble or need help, without having to strain your voice.” It also carries further, he says, adding that many people he knows take whistles with them when they leave the house. “Say you’re stuck in an elevator — you to be able to blow a whistle. It’s soothing just to have on you.”

This four-in-one emergency tool is also critical to have on hand, our experts say, in the event you need to turn off your gas valves or water meters (it can also be used to pry open doors or cabinets).

Two of our experts cited an emergency radio as an essential part of any blackout kit. Coby Coonradt and Cameron Hardy, hosts of The Casual Preppers podcast, explain that because the radio is “powered by battery, solar, or hand crank, it can be ready to use at any unexpected moment.”

And while people tend to stock up on essentials like food and water, they “often forget to include things that will make themselves more comfortable,” says Schaffer. He recommends adding in seasonally appropriate items that will help you manage different temperatures if your heat or air-conditioning goes out. For the winter, that means sleeping bags, like this expert-recommended one from The North Face.

And here’s a self-inflating pad to go under it.

Schaffer says, “If you are a person who relies heavily on your phone for entertainment, make sure you have things on hand so you can entertain people (and especially kids) appropriately.” Goodwin keeps games and playing cards stocked in his kit for this express purpose.

entry.title: The Best Martini Glasses, According to Bartenders
entry.summary: The options have evolved since the 1980s cone.
entry.content:
Technically speaking, you can drink a martini out of any glass. But having a great martini in a perfect martini glass is a specific kind of delight. No matter how you like your martini — with gin or vodka, with a twist or an olive (or both), bracingly dry or with a more generous pour of vermouth — the best martini glass is one that looks great, keeps your martini cold for as long as possible, and is a pleasure to hold and drink from.

Martini glassware has evolved beyond the ubiquitous ’80s-style cone glasses — though those have their retro charms — into many different designs. There’s even an insulated and portable version for all your outdoor martini needs. A martini glass isn’t limited to just serving martinis. You can use it for all manner of cocktails, from a classic Manhattan to a Vesper to a Cosmopolitan.

To find the best martini glasses, I talked to beverage directors, bartenders, and cocktail experts, who all had picks for their favorite vessel. If you’re looking for more cocktail paraphernalia, we also have recommendations for coupe glasses, which are preferred for martinis by many cocktail experts, as well as guides to highball glasses and cocktail picks.

Updated on November 17, 2026
All the recommendations below have been updated with the latest pricing and availability.

“My favorite glass for a classic martini has got to be a Nick and Nora, straight from the freezer,” says Tony Abou-Ganim, author of The Modern Mixologist. He’s not the only one. A Nick and Nora, with its elegant profile, is a favorite of several cocktail professionals that I spoke to, including the creator of Hendricks Gin and owner of Tamworth Distilling, Steven Grasse, whose “at-home go-to glassware is a vintage Nick and Nora glass.”

Abou-Ganim prefers this Minners glass from Steelite International, and it’s available in bulk from many online restaurant-supply stores. “The size and feel of the glass is both elegant and functional with a touch of style and nostalgia,” Abou-Ganim says. “I love to serve it with a small carafe on the side over crushed ice, which keeps my martini ice cold without any added dilution from the first sip to the last.”

Paul MacDonald, bartender at Friday Saturday Sunday, loves a coupe more than a traditional triangular martini glass. “I’m happy that we’ve managed to reclaim both style and function in a martini with properly round-bottomed, tapered coupes that facilitate drinking rather than spilling,” he says. His favorite is this etched version.

Coupes are also a favorite of My Loup bartender Jillian Moore, who prefers to use them when drinking at home to “avoid breakage.” Her vote is for a martini glass on the larger side. “To me, larger glasses are by default easier to maneuver and require less dexterity than a smaller glass,” Moore says. These Libbey coupe glasses, at nine ounces each, offer a little bit more room and heft, if you worry about spilling.

John Winterman, the owner-operator of Francie, where there’s a mean martini on the menu, also loves a coupe, though he admits, “I will quaff a martini out of almost anything that holds four ounces of liquid.” For his at-home libations, however, “only one glass is perfect for me.” He reaches for the exquisite Lobmeyr Patrician Champagne Coupe, made by a company founded in Vienna in 1823 that provided glassware to the Imperial Court. “The glasses are hand blown, and careful inspection reveals subtle differences from one coupe to another. There is an ethereal lightness to them, as though one had captured the air itself,” Winterman says.

For a more traditional martini glass, particularly if you like one with a bit of flair, Wilson recommends these Estelle glasses. “The extra-long stem is beautiful and looks and feels so elegant. I have the amber-smoke color, and I think the color is stunning,” she says.

If your heart is set on the conical, old-fashioned martini glasses popular in the ’80s and ’90s, look no further than the Rona. Moore votes for reclaiming the shape: “I would like to bring back punch-bowl, Sex and the City-size martini glasses,” she says. “There is something so ridiculous about them that I think the visual is almost as important as the drink in the glass. That and the fact that I would never have to worry about spilling the drink on myself.” They’re also a favorite of Elle Gourmet Canada editorial director Erin McLaughlin, who thinks the shape makes you slow down and sip the martini. Plus you need “core strength to lift it,” says McLaughlin.

This martini glass, recommended by Sam Clark, the creative director of beverage at Fairmont Banff Springs, is midway between a Nick and Nora glass and a classic coupe. Clark calls the LSA Borough Martini glass’s curved shape “perfect for aerating a martini or cocktail to enjoy the flavor of the spirit with a subtle shape difference from the classic V.” He particularly likes the rim of the glass, which is thin and delicate, “creating a seamless liquid-to-mouth experience that thicker glassware simply cannot,” alongside the long stem which ensures that the warmth of your hand won’t interfere with the temperature of the cocktail. But the best part is that despite looking elegant and fragile, these glasses are dishwasher safe.

This list is a product of my preoccupation with the toy industry that surges each year between Valentine’s Day and Halloween. Over the course of those eightish months, I visit toy fairs, test the newest toy releases, and take meetings with dozens of toy experts, from teachers and nannies to trend forecasters and stylish parents. I also make sure to pay attention to the toys that keep showing up at playgrounds, on social-media feeds, and in my group chats with my friends and colleagues who are parents.

The biggest toy trend in 2026 has been squishies, from NeeDoh Nice Cubes to slow-rising sticks of butter and glittery blind-box dumplings. It’s the 30th anniversary of Pokémon, and the trading cards and other collectibles are more popular (and potentially valuable) than ever. And oddly enough, hacky sacks saw a major comeback among tweens, teens, and college students. Below, you’ll find the most asked-for (and at times hard to get) toys of the 2026 holiday season.

Melissa & Doug’s soft-serve ice-cream machine is one of my favorite new toys of the year. Kids load two flavors into the top of the dispenser, then press a button and watch them twist together and drop into the waiting cone.

Clickeez fidgets look like the keys on a computer keyboard but cuter. They make a satisfying clickety-clackety sound when you press them, and this particularly popular set comes with 12 blind-box fidgets to start a collection plus a keyboard-shaped organizer tray to display it. It has already sold out and come back in stock multiple times; plan to sign up for restock alerts and refresh product pages often to have a chance at buying it at the $33 retail price.

When the original Air Toobz launched in 2023, it was such a huge hit that it sold out several times over. This year, maker Fat Brain Toys released Air Toobz Evo, a slightly less expensive upgrade that offers the same open-ended play. Inside the portable console, there’s an adjustable fan that lets kids experiment with different wind speeds. On the lowest setting the foam balls might hover over the end of a tube, whereas on the highest setting they are launched across the room.

In the world of mini magnetic tiles, Connetix are my favorite thanks to extra-strong magnets that allow for stronger builds and prevent tiles from falling and getting lost under car seats or restaurant booths.

This Paw Patrol truck is part of the merch collection tied to the latest movie that came out in August. The dino on the back pops up and fills with air at the press of a button; then kids can remove it and roll it around on the wheels under its feet.

At the end of its gory hatching, kids have a 16-inch Megalodon with light-up eyes and chomping teeth. And they can repeat the big reveal over and over again by just adding water.

The newest Tickle Me Elmo doll is 18 inches tall and more giggly than ever. Plus its arms move and its mouth opens and closes with each tickle.

VTech’s brand new toy guitar is designed for children 5 years old and up. A complement to the brand’s drum pad and DJ mixer, it has interactive strings, light-up frets, and four different guitar styles. Kids can build a band by adding or removing drum beats, piano riffs, and additional guitar sounds or play a rhythm game by tapping the whammy bar in time. (For flashier mini musicians, it also comes in pink.)

The landline revolution has given parents a compelling alternative to smartphones and watches, especially for elementary-school kids. And now Tin Can is making it easier for young landline users to keep track of each other’s numbers. The Rolodex-style Contact Keeper is weighted with a grippy silicone pad on the bottom to keep it from sliding around, and the cards are removable so kids can trade them like business cards. In addition to the contact keeper, Tin Can just came out with a limited-edition (and very on-trend) transparent phone and charms for decorating the curly cord.

Read more: ‘Is Grandma Home?’ Our Kids Love Yapping Away on Tin Can’s Landline.

Waffle’s landline phone comes with a curly cord but can be used cordless so kids can talk while roaming around the house. It also has caller ID and lets you add one non-Waffle number to your contacts list for free. The company also makes a GPS-enabled phone called the Waffle Go that lets kids call or send voice messages to their grownups from outside the home.

Earlier this year, teens and college kids went nuts for this quintessential ’90s toy. And Razor’s three-pack would make a great stocking stuffer for siblings.

The Zelda 40th-anniversary edition Nintendo Switch 2 is currently sold out, but it’s been restocking in waves. Keep refreshing the product pages at Nintendo, Gamestop, Target, and Walmart and sign up for restock alerts where you can, and hopefully you’ll be able to get your hands on one before Christmas. (Note that the regular Switch 2 console that launched last year is readily available, and would also make an excellent gift paired with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which critics have called one of the best new video games of 2026.)

Finally some good Warrior Cats merch, a few years after the book series went viral among middle-school readers.

Super Smalls recently launched this sparkly journal that kids can cover with 3-D gem stickers. To keep out prying eyes, it comes complete with a combination lock.

Although it looks like a blender, Mark Rober’s Crunchinator contraption is built to crush everyday objects like soda cans, raw eggs, yogurt cups, and random toys. It comes with three crusher bits and a wrench to help kids apply brute force. It’s already starting to sell out, so if you want one, don’t wait.

entry.title: Are Any of The Fancy New Boxed Mac and Cheeses Better Than Annie’s?
entry.summary: We taste tested eight varieties and came out with two winners.
entry.content:
Like jarred tomato sauce, boxed macaroni and cheese is a pantry staple. Whether you make it for your kids after a busy day at work or doctor it up with bacon and broccoli for a nostalgic, comforting dinner for yourself, it’s always there, and it’s always easy. But also like jarred tomato sauce, the market is pretty big, and many new options have come out in the last few years, so I was curious to find out if any in particular stood out as the best.

I wanted to start with a ubiquitous and time-tested brand in order to have a solid point of reference to compare some newer ones to. Kraft and Annie’s are both, in their own ways, that — and after polling my colleagues, it became clear allegiances are split. New York deputy editor Alexis Swerdloff put it well: “Kraft was probably the classic benchmark, but Annie’s has become that in the last decade or so.” As such, I decided to proceed with Annie’s and then call in a handful of others to taste-test alongside.

I went with a mix of orange cheddar and white cheddar versions, plus a couple made with Parmesan, and one more distinct outlier: the option closest to mac and cheese from Riff, a very new boxed pasta company by acclaimed chef Daniel Humm. It was a bit of a vibes-based curation, but I also put a few guardrails in place to keep things somewhat consistent. I didn’t test anything gluten-free (but that may be the subject of a future taste test); and despite the directions for some calling for low-fat milk and optional butter (presumably to keep the calorie count lower), I used whole milk and added butter for each (except one that specifically only has you use water and its powdered cheese mix).

I also called back senior editor Winnie Yang and senior writer Michael Zhao to taste with me. We considered real cheesiness level (or, on the other end of the spectrum, if it leaned processed-tasting), sauce texture, coating ability, pasta shape, and pasta texture. Below: our findings.

Beyond his restaurants, cookbook writing, and acting, Matty Matheson also has a food company, which launched in 2023. It sells seasoning mixes, dressings, barbecue sauces, and boxed mac and cheeses. I was especially excited about this one, as it felt the coolest of the bunch (small thing, but I do love the packaging). We tried both the Sharp Cheddar and the cheddar-based Original (which isn’t available for purchase in the U.S. right now, so I’ll focus on the Sharp Cheddar). Unfortunately, to say it underdelivered is an understatement. (Wildly, I feel I must note up here that another flavor from the brand was one of our very favorites, but more on that below.) It was really the only macaroni and cheese that all three of us taste-testers had an immediate adverse response to — so much so that we could hardly go in for a second bite. To sum it up: Zhao noted that it tasted like plastic. (And in case the Original ever becomes available here, we also did not like that one — it had an overpowering mustard flavor.)

Riff is the aforementioned outlier. The company, founded by chef Daniel Humm, launched only a couple of months ago, and the lineup is boxed pastas more than boxed macaroni and cheeses. There’s Sesame Ginger Noodles, Coconut Curry Noodles, Spicy Tomato Rigatoni, Garlic Lemon Rotini, and this Creamy Parmesan Cavatappi — the closest to standard macaroni and cheese. In fact, it’s similar: dried pasta, to which you add a sauce made from milk, butter, and the included cheese-seasoning packet. (It does call for about three times as much milk as the other ones we tried, requiring more reduction once you marry all the ingredients together on the stovetop.) The major differences are that the pasta is full-size, and it comes with a small packet of breadcrumbs for sprinkling on top. The brand also explicitly encourages riffing — hence the name — by adding extra ingredients like mushrooms, lemon juice, and chopped parsley (though I would argue all boxed macaroni and cheeses are ripe for such additions).

We were a bit let down by this one. It was fine enough, which is to say not as immediately off-putting at the Matheson Company Sharp Cheddar (and we did all enjoy the provided breadcrumbs). But there were clearly dried alliums added to the seasoning mix, which tasted dominant, and took it into dehydrated soup mix territory. It lacked the bright, tangy cheesiness we were looking for.

Both Annie’s cheddar elbows and white cheddar shells were totally solid, and we had a slight preference towards the latter. Turns out, there’s a reason we used these as a benchmark. They’re both mild, if a little flat — but certainly completely inoffensive, and — in a good way — nostalgic-tasting. The sauce on these is on the looser side.

Goodles emerged on the scene in 2021 and has become pretty ubiquitous, given how new it is (while I wouldn’t say it’s as much so as Annie’s or Kraft, the reach is far). Its noodles have some added protein from ingredients like chickpeas (though with the exception of a few designated gluten-free varieties, they include wheat flour), and added nutrients extracted from foods like kale, sunflower seeds, and mushrooms. Surprisingly, you truly can’t tell. I was impressed with the taste and texture, which were comparable to regular noodles. (In the case of the elbows, they were a bit bigger in size than Annie’s, but nothing noticeable when taking bites.)

The cheddar elbows in particular are another unobjectionable pick that also tasted somewhat nostalgic, despite it being a newer brand. This one leans slightly tangier and a bit saltier than the Annie’s version, and the sauce is a bit thicker, too. While Yang had a slight preference for Annie’s (“though I honestly can’t quite figure out why,” she noted), both Zhao and I found them pretty interchangeable. We’d be happy to eat either, if a bit uninspired.

Boss Cow stands out in a couple of ways. The company touts their ingredients: unenriched organic durum wheat semolina past from Italy, dairy from regenerative family farms, and no preservatives. It’s also the only boxed macaroni and cheese we tried that has you make a sauce from just their cheese seasoning and water — no added milk or butter. I’m impressed by the better-for-you ingredients, and that the sauce method turned out truly creamy results. The sauce has a distinct tang — more so than any of the others we tried. Unfortunately, Yang and I both found that the initial hit of sauce slid off, such that we were left with distinct plain boiled noodle taste, bite after bite. Zhao, however, was more impressed: “You could sprinkle a crumb topping on it, throw it in the oven for 10 minutes, and no one would know it was coming from a box,” he said.

Goodles’ white cheddar version stood out for a few reasons. We liked the shell pasta shape better than traditional elbows, thanks to their sauce-holding ability. This was true across the board, but the Goodles sauce also had a distinct cheese pull — I could see it in the pot as I stirred — that helped coat the noodles especially well. And crucially, the cheese taste here was especially clean, sharp, and savory, rather than being more vaguely dairy-like, as was the case with the milder Annie’s. Indeed, Yang said: “It tastes like a more elevated Annie’s.”

We’ve come full circle with this one. Despite our overtly negative feelings about the Matheson Food Company sharp cheddar flavor, the Pep Pep Macaroni — basically a version of cacio e pepe — was distinctly delicious. Really, it was the very favorite of the bunch. Again, the real cheese flavor here played a big role. It actually tasted like Parmesan balanced by a subtle, warm background kick of black pepper. It kept us going in, bite after bite — not too spicy or overwhelming, but still distinct. I also liked the pasta shape (something I didn’t even have the pleasure of noticing with the other one): small and ditalini-like, a real pleasure to shovel into your mouth.

entry.title: 125 Carefully Selected, Unusually Special Gifts Under $200
entry.summary: Featuring a cedar bat house, a three-foot tall taper, and perimenopausal American Girls.
entry.content:
Has gift shopping become an even more daunting process lately? We’re inundated with gift guides starting the second the last Halloween candy wrapper is swept off the sidewalk, then chased around Instagram by brands that may or may not be AI slop. There is just so much stuff out there — everyone’s disrupted everything, your deli down the street now sells merch, and even the most obscure Danish house museum has a Shopify storefront. Faced with truly endless options of buyable things on the internet, we pick an item for this annual print gift issue like we’re the judges on American Idol: When we see it, we know it. Whether that’s a pair of purple socks, a stuffed mallard, or a Claudiosaurus fossil.

The products below went through an arduous journey to be here. The work begins early in the year, when we make our first bookmarks. After we tap into the Strategist hive mind of editors and writers to compile a list of more than 600 ideas, items that are new this year or unusual enough to be worthy of inclusion, we cut about a quarter of those over the next few months, then make even more eliminations (and additions) with each round of tweaking to gather the products you’ll find in this issue. Given how many come from teeny boutiques or are limited editions, items are constantly selling out, which makes producing this guide a bit like a game of Whac-a-Mole — and often leads to heartbreak. We found one editor with his head in his hands after he learned Sascha the stuffed schnauzer was no longer available.

Tucked into this year’s catalogue are interviews with designers of select gifts we wanted to know more about. We spoke to the creator of a viral dog collar, a snail wrangler, an artist who forms vases from pressed flowers, and the maker of a cast-bronze toilet-paper holder — all to learn more about their creations and who would be most delighted to receive them as a gift.

We’ve divided the 393 gifts that made the cut into three categories — under $50, $50 to $199, and $200 and up. Below, you’ll find our favorite gift ideas from $50 to $199. And if you haven’t found what you’re looking for, peruse the many other gift guides the staff of the Strategist has made for you here.

What does a head snail wrangler actually do?
I think it’s funny because it conjures up an image of multiple people wrangling snails. But my job encompasses just about every part of the business, from taking care of the snails in our greenhouse — which involves feeding, watering, sorting, and general greenhouse maintenance — to the production side of things. I am the owner of the business and therefore the head snail wrangler.

What is the cycle of raising snails until they’re ready for processing?
We start with a wild batch. The species we raise — Cornu aspersum, or petit gris — exists here in the continental United States, but it is a nonnative invasive species. We do all of our own breeding and egg laying, and we do everything here in our greenhouse. Their life cycle is about six to nine months from egg to maturity, and we get them to lay twice a year.

How do these snails taste?
We wanted these to taste like Long Island, so they’re fed a lot of wild greens from the area. These are things we can get, at least spring through fall, from our surroundings, like clover, dandelion, burdock, sorrel, and wild -carrot. Some are invasive species — like garlic mustard, for instance — and the snails just really enjoy eating them. So a lot of their diet is made up of these wild greens, which in turn has a big impact on the final flavor. They taste very herbaceous, very vegetal, whereas a canned snail, I think, is just kind of a bland piece of protein.

What’s your favorite thing to eat and drink alongside a dish of escargot?
My favorite preparation is the babbalucci, which consists of in-shell snails that are stewed. It’s a hearty stew of snails, garlic, onion, tomato, and red wine, and you stew it all down for about a half an hour, 45 minutes, and then serve it with some crusty bread, some toothpicks for picking the meat out. It’s a really fun way to eat them, but it is messy, and that’s part of the fun of it.

Why different soccer jerseys for different neighborhoods?
These shirts were made exclusively for the Brooklyn Champions Cup, a soccer tournament featuring ten Brooklyn neighborhoods in collaboration with Brooklyn Org and the Footy League.

Are there any specific references in the designs?
On the Flatbush jersey, there’s a reference to an Italian league jersey from the ’90s, a team called Parma. The Bushwick and Williamsburg kits have a design that’s split down the middle. Tons of teams have used that same design across the history of the sport, but for me, it’s a reference to the 2008 Barcelona kit, which is the year Pep Guardiola became the head coach and created perhaps the most successful team in the history of the sport. The photographs we referenced for Bed-Stuy came from a project called Documerica, and the images were of the Kosciuszko Pool in the 1970s. The colors were part of Brooklyn Org’s brand and reminded me of the pool, which I bike next to often. At night, it has this foamy blue when you’re just going through it as the sun’s setting. For the others, we were just trying to find the energy that fit.

Mayor Mamdani made the NYC World Cup jerseys you manufactured go a bit viral this summer. Did you get to meet him?
The mayor invited us to Gracie Mansion for a pickup soccer game as a thank-you for producing the World Cup jerseys. It was the day the World Cup was starting, and we were releasing the jerseys, so we played. That’s when I realized how out of shape I am. He was a forward. It was really cool seeing him. And then he took off his shoes, so he was playing barefoot. I’m like, Yo, he’s gangster.

What prompted you to want to design your own pieces?
It wasn’t so much like, I want to be a designer. I wouldn’t consider myself that at all. Essentially, I would say I am a writer who created a shirt. I like to do live shopping, and I want to sell things that I 150 percent believe in, and that might include incredible vintage pieces. I speak on behalf of other brands and promote small labels. And I finally was just like, You know what? I’m going to do it for myself.

What inspired the shirt?
It’s based on a vintage Tom Ford–era Gucci shirt that I accidentally washed. Since having a kid, sometimes stuff goes a bit haywire, so maybe I’ll throw a shirt on top of the hamper and bring it to the dry cleaner after. This time, that wasn’t the case, and I threw it into the washer and dryer and ruined it. I really wore the shirt to death.

What about this type of shirt did you like?
I’m not a fashion person in the sense of you’re never going to see me experimenting with a crazy Comme des Garçons silhouette or Simone Rocha. I’m a “one plus one equals two” type of girl. I lead a very busy life — everyone does—but I take care of the kid and then I have to go to a meeting and then I have to do something on-camera and it’s a whirlwind. So I have always worn clothes that can transition. A lot of them have the same sort of boatneck cut that I like. And with this piece, I made it more of a boatneck. It’s something I wear undone and closed and whatever I feel like. And then I created it in Engorged, which is this juicy, ready-to-burst, bottom-of-the-orange-juice-box-pulp hue, and Cat Tongue, a pink. And then the other color is Midnight at Brighton Beach, which is just basically my Slavic euphemism for black.
